metadata.title: How Google Docs Lets Two People Type in the Same Sentence
metadata.narration_policy: Narration is SCRIPT.md verbatim, one script section per beat. Beat IDs B01-B10 match script sections 1-10; BVDT, BHTF and BOUT are sections 11, 12 and 13. On-screen-only lines and source tags in SCRIPT.md are not narrated.
metadata.visual_policy: Simple illustrative graphics only: two plain browser windows, the letters a b c, operations moving to a server, a revision log, cursors, two copies that change on their own and end up the same. No Google logo, no Google Docs interface screenshots or colour scheme, no other branding. The windows are drawn rectangles with a text line, not a copy of any product's interface. Every example is an illustration, not data. The Claude composer, verdict page and channel mark are redrawn bookends, not screenshots.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Keya, and this video is about how Google Docs lets two people type in the same sentence. The voice you're hearing is an AI voice reading my script.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hi, Keya'
three result lines land: your change goes to a server, other people's changes are shifted to fit, every copy ends up the same
the AI-voice disclosure is spoken while the answered composer holds

props.segment: How Google Docs Lets Two People Type in the Same Sentence
props.command: Explain how Google Docs lets two people type in the same sentence.
props.runningText: thinking about two people and one sentence…
output: Your change goes to a server
Other people's changes are shifted to fit
Every copy ends up the same

beats.narration_text: I've worked with shared documents. Sometimes two people type in the same line, and the text overlaps for a moment. So I wondered: if I press Control Z, will I undo my teammate's work too? I tested it in two windows. It only undid mine. How does Google Docs keep track?

shot.visual_intent: Two plain drawn windows side by side, each holding the same line of text. A terracotta cursor types in the left window and a teal cursor types in the right; for a moment the two bits of text overlap in the line. A Ctrl+Z key chip lands in the left window; only the terracotta words disappear and the teal words stay. A question mark settles over the gap between the windows: 'How does it keep track?'. No Google logo, no Docs interface.

show.event: two plain windows draw in, each with the same line of text; 'shared document' reads small above them
two cursors type into the same line at once and the two bits of text overlap for a moment on 'overlaps for a moment'
a Ctrl+Z key chip presses in the left window on 'if I press Control Z'; a question mark floats up: 'my teammate's work too?'
only the left window's words disappear; the right window's words stay, on 'It only undid mine'
the question 'How does it keep track?' lands between the windows

beats.note: Keya's own experience and test (tagged in SCRIPT.md). The windows are drawn rectangles, not the product's interface.

beats.narration_text: Google Docs doesn't let the last person win. It merges every change, so everyone ends up with the same document. Let's see how, step by step.

show.event: the writer types 'The last person to type wins.' in terracotta, finishing before the 50% point
it pauses, then deletes the whole sentence
'Every keystroke gets merged.' types in ink
the corrected sentence holds while the voice says 'Let's see how, step by step'

props.text:
The last person
to type wins.
props.triggerWords: The last person to type wins

beats.note: Typed 'The last person to type wins.' then corrected to 'Every keystroke gets merged.' The whole sentence is the trigger phrase so the correction replaces the sentence, not one word. No lead silence, as in the week 5 film: audio and typing start together. Narration now ends 'so everyone ends up with the same document'. Keystrokes cannot go faster than one frame, so both on-screen sentences are kept short. 'The last person to type wins' is the viewer's likely misconception, not a claim about how Google Docs once worked. The typed text is split over two short lines so the whole correction finishes typing before the 50% frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's why this is hard. Say the document says a, b, c. At the same moment, I add an x at the start, and my teammate deletes the third letter, c. My x pushes everything one place to the right, so the third letter is now b. If my teammate's change is applied exactly as it was sent, the wrong letter gets deleted.

shot.visual_intent: A row of three letter tiles a, b, c with slot numbers 1, 2, 3 under them. Two actors act at the same moment: 'me' drops an x tile in at the start, 'teammate' points a delete arrow at the third tile, c. The x pushes the row one place right, so the third slot now holds b. The teammate's delete, applied as sent, lands on b: b is crossed out in terracotta and 'wrong letter' appears. Labelled 'illustrative example'.

show.event: 'Why this is hard' lands; three tiles a, b, c draw in with slot numbers 1 2 3 beneath
two labels appear at once, 'me: add x at the start' and 'teammate: delete the third letter', with an arrow on c
the x tile drops in at the front and the a, b, c tiles slide one place right; the slot numbers stay put, so slot 3 now sits under b
the teammate's delete arrow, unchanged, lands on b and crosses it out in terracotta: 'wrong letter'; c is left standing

beats.note: Illustrative example, and the same a-b-c shape the Wikipedia article on operational transformation uses (insert at the start, delete the third character). See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: When you open a Google Doc, it runs in two places: in your browser, and on Google's server. As you type, your browser doesn't send the whole document. It sends only your changes to the server, and receives everyone else's changes back.

shot.visual_intent: Two plain boxes: 'your browser' on the left holding a small page, 'the server' on the right. Between them, small change packets (insert x, delete c) travel from the browser to the server; the page itself never moves. Other people's packets travel back and land on the page. Under the browser a short two-line list reads 'changes not yet sent' and 'sent, not yet acknowledged'; under the server 'changes received', 'revision log', 'current document'. The list is secondary and drawn small. No Google logo.

show.event: two boxes draw in, 'your browser' and 'the server', each holding a small page; 'runs in two places' lands
the page does not move; one small packet 'insert x' leaves the browser for the server on 'sends only your changes'
a packet from someone else travels back and lands on the browser's page on 'receives everyone else's changes back'
the small lists settle under each box: what the browser keeps, what the server keeps

beats.note: The lists under each box follow Google's blog post (what each client and the server keep track of). The blog says the code runs in your browser and on Google's servers (plural); the script says 'server', a simplification. See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: Google's engineers explained that Docs solves this with a technique called operational transformation. Each edit is an operation, like "insert x at the start" or "delete the third letter." When two operations clash, one is transformed to fit the other. My teammate's delete is shifted from the third letter to the fourth, so the c is deleted, just as they meant.

shot.visual_intent: The same a, b, c tiles, now with two operation chips above: 'insert x at the start' and 'delete the third letter'. The two chips clash, a small diamond labelled 'transform' sits between them, and the delete chip rewrites itself to 'delete the fourth letter' while its arrow slides from slot 3 to slot 4. The x is in, the arrow lands on c, and c is removed, leaving x a b. The word 'operational transformation' sits as the label of the diamond.

show.event: the words 'operational transformation' land; the a, b, c tiles return
two operation chips appear, 'insert x at the start' and 'delete the third letter', as 'each edit is an operation' is spoken
the chips clash; a diamond labelled 'transform' opens between them and the delete chip is rewritten to fit the insert
the delete arrow slides from slot 3 to slot 4 on 'from the third letter to the fourth', lands on c, and c is removed: x a b

beats.note: Narration now begins 'Google's engineers explained that Docs solves this with...', because the sources are old blog posts. No visual change.

beats.narration_text: But transforming isn't enough. Every copy also needs the same changes, in the same order. That's the second part, the collaboration protocol. The server processes changes in the order they arrive. It sends an acknowledgement back to the person who made the change, passes the change on to everyone else, and keeps every change in a revision log: the complete history of the document.

shot.visual_intent: A server column in the middle with two editors, 'me' and 'teammate', on the sides. Two change packets arrive at the server one after the other and take numbers 1 and 2 in a stack on the server called 'revision log: the complete history'. For each packet, the sender gets a small check ('acknowledged') and the other editor gets the change passed on. The stack of the log keeps growing; nothing leaves it. No names from the blog example.

show.event: 'transforming isn't enough' lands; a server column draws between two editors, 'me' and 'teammate'
two packets arrive at the server; the first to arrive is numbered 1, the second 2, on 'in the order they arrive'
for each packet the sender gets a check 'acknowledged' and the other editor receives the change
both changes sit stacked in the server's 'revision log: the complete history of the document'

beats.note: The acknowledgement goes to the editor who sent the change; the change itself goes to the others. The narration now says so, and the scene draws it that way.

beats.narration_text: In my test, Control Z only undid my own typing, so the document must keep track of who made each change. I can also see where my teammate's cursor is. And sometimes their text shows up a moment late, because each change has to travel to the server and back.

shot.visual_intent: One plain window with a line of text. Each typed letter carries a tiny coloured underline for who typed it: terracotta for me, teal for my teammate. Ctrl+Z removes only the terracotta letters. A teal cursor with a small 'teammate' tag sits in the line. Then a short path to a server box and back: a teal letter leaves the teammate, travels up and down, and lands in my line a beat after the cursor. 'In my test' sits small at the top.

show.event: 'In my test' lands; a window draws in with a typed line, each letter underlined in the colour of whoever typed it
Ctrl+Z presses and only the terracotta letters vanish on 'only undid my own typing'; a tag 'who made each change?' appears, marked 'my guess'
a teal cursor with a 'teammate' tag slides into the line on 'where my teammate's cursor is'
a teal letter travels to a small server box and back and lands a beat after the cursor, on 'a moment late'

beats.note: Keya's own experience and test (tagged in SCRIPT.md). 'The document must keep track of who made each change' is Keya's inference from her test, not a claim about Google's internals, so the scene marks the who-made-it layer 'my guess'.

beats.narration_text: There's another approach I'm just starting to learn about, called CRDTs, short for conflict-free replicated data types. Each copy can be changed on its own, at the same time, without coordinating with the others, and the copies still end up the same.

shot.visual_intent: 'Just starting to learn' sits small at the top. Two copies of the same short line sit side by side with no server between them. Each copy is changed on its own, at the same moment: the left copy gains a terracotta letter, the right copy gains a teal letter. No messages are sent first and there are no ID tags. Then the two changes cross over and both copies end on the identical line. Labelled 'simplified'.

show.event: 'CRDT: conflict-free replicated data type' lands; 'I'm just starting to learn' appears small

two copies of the same line draw in side by side; each copy is changed on its own, at the same time: a terracotta letter appears in the left copy and a teal letter in the right, with no message passing first, on 'changed on its own, at the same time'
a dashed 'no coordination' gap holds between the two copies on 'without coordinating with the others'
the two changes cross over and both copies end on the identical line: 'the copies still end up the same'; 'simplified' appears small

beats.note: Keya flags she has not studied CRDTs deeply and the narration says so. The wording follows Wikipedia only (updated independently, concurrently and without coordination; the copies converge). No ID tags and no 'any order' claim. Listen-check the pronunciation of 'CRDTs'.

beats.narration_text: It isn't perfect. In my experience, on a slow connection, text can appear late, or overlap for a moment before it settles. And if two people rewrite the same sentence in different ways, the system can merge both edits, but it can't decide which wording the team actually wanted.

shot.visual_intent: Left panel: a window and a long dotted path to a server box; a letter crawls along the path, so the teammate's text appears late, then slips into the line and settles. Right panel: two different rewrites of the same short sentence, one terracotta, one teal, both kept in the line side by side. A question mark sits over them: 'which wording did the team want?'. 'In my experience' sits small at the top of the left panel; the right panel is labelled 'framing, not a measurement'.

show.event: 'In my experience' lands; a long dotted path to a server box draws in, and a letter crawls along it
the late letter overlaps the line for a moment, then settles, on 'overlap for a moment before it settles'
the right panel opens: one sentence, rewritten two ways by two people, a terracotta version and a teal version
both rewrites stay merged in the line side by side; a question mark lands: 'which wording did the team want?'

beats.note: Keya's own experience (tagged in SCRIPT.md). 'Can merge both edits but can't decide which wording was wanted' is framing, not a measured claim; the on-screen label says so.

beats.narration_text: So how does Google Docs let two people type in the same sentence? It doesn't avoid conflicts. It fixes them so fast that we almost never notice. Behind every keystroke, changes are shifted, ordered and shared. And when I pressed Control Z, only my words disappeared.

show.event: the artifact page opens on the title
the heading lands: shifted, ordered and shared
the closing line lands: only my words disappeared
